findings.source_passage: upon the great canal of Hang-Ho, or whatever they call it, in China, four or five laborers on the foot-path will draw a bulky freighted junk at the rate of a mile an hour; but this grand argosy we towed heavily forged along, as if laden with pig-lead in bulk
findings.why_it_matters: This is a rhetorically distinctive digression—playful, bathetic, and voice-defining—that establishes the chapter's ironic register before the whale-supper comedy begins. Its complete absence flattens the opening.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Hang-Ho / pig-lead comparison in the opening towing paragraph, even if slightly condensed; it is the chapter's first signature moment.

findings.source_passage: they are the invariable outriders of all slave ships crossing the Atlantic, systematically trotting alongside, to be handy in case a parcel is to be carried anywhere, or a dead slave to be decently buried
findings.source_locator: long shark-digression paragraph, fourth 'and though' clause
findings.why_it_matters: This is one of Melville's most charged anti-slavery insertions in the novel; critical tradition returns to it as an example of his moral politics embedded in apparent digression. The draft reduces the entire slave-ship clause to the bare phrase 'slave-ships,' erasing all of the specific language.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the slave-ship clause verbatim or near-verbatim within the shark digression: 'invariable outriders of all slave ships crossing the Atlantic, systematically trotting alongside, to be handy in case a parcel is to be carried anywhere, or a dead slave to be decently buried.'

findings.source_passage: You must go home and be born over again; you don't know how to cook a whale-steak yet… Born in a ferry-boat! That's queer, too… 'Hind de hatchway, in ferry-boat, goin' ober de Roanoke
findings.why_it_matters: The 'born over again' exchange and the Roanoke ferry-boat detail are among the chapter's most comic and voice-establishing passages; they also carry interpretive weight regarding Fleece's identity and the chapter's burlesque sermon frame. The draft reduces the entire exchange to 'cross-questioned him on age and birthplace.'
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the dialogue: age question, 'born over again' punchline, and the Roanoke/'hind de hatchway' answer—these are compact enough to include without significant word-count cost.

findings.source_passage: this old Fleece, as they called him, came shuffling and limping along, assisting his step with his tongs… this old Ebony floundered along
findings.why_it_matters: Melville's triple-repetition structure ('this old Fleece… this old Ebony…') is a deliberate stylistic device that enacts Fleece's laborious progress; the knee-pans joke ('which he did not keep well scoured like his other pans') is also cut. The draft condenses this to a single clause.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the triple-anaphoric structure and the knee-pans wordplay; both are brief enough to include and are essential to the comic texture of the entrance.

findings.source_passage: huge globular pieces of the whale of the bigness of a human head
findings.why_it_matters: 'Of the bigness of a human head' is a specific, unsettling image that gives the shark feast its horror; reducing it to 'huge globular pieces' loses the human-scale comparison that makes the detail memorable.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'of the bigness of a human head' in the sharks-feeding sentence.

findings.source_passage: that's your gizzard! Aloft! aloft!—that's it—now you have it. Hold it there now, and pay attention
findings.source_locator: Stubb's 'hold your hat' orders, late in the Stubb–Fleece dialogue
findings.why_it_matters: The gizzard/heart comedy—where Stubb corrects Fleece's hand position and mistakes his gizzard for his heart—is a distinctive burlesque moment that amplifies the sermon parody; its absence leaves the instruction-giving sequence flat.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the gizzard exchange (it is short) between the 'drop your tongs' line and the steak instructions.

findings.source_passage: Best cooked 'teak I eber taste; joosy, berry joosy
findings.source_locator: after Stubb commands Fleece to taste the steak
findings.why_it_matters: Fleece's 'joosy, berry joosy' line is one of the chapter's small comic peaks and ironically reverses Stubb's complaint; its absence removes a punchline that the tasting scene exists to deliver.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the tasting exchange: Stubb holding tongs toward Fleece, Fleece smacking his withered lips, and the 'joosy, berry joosy' line.

summary: The draft contains three high-severity losses (Hang-Ho canal comparison, slave-ships passage, 'born over again' exchange) plus four medium-severity losses (Fleece's triple-anaphoric entrance, 'bigness of a human head,' gizzard comedy, 'joosy berry joosy'), gutting both the chapter's comic texture and its most interpretively charged passage.
